note: Areas and arrows are approximate reconstructions from campaign maps and the ancient narratives. The base map is corrected with occupied areas where it lags (for example the south of Italy after Cannae); a moving circle marks the ground held by a marching army. Days within a year are often approximate, because ancient sources give seasons.

chapters.title: Over the Alps
arrows: Hannibal's march from New Carthage over the Alps to the Taurini (218 BCE)
Gnaeus Scipio lands at Emporion (218 BCE)
Hannibal advances to the Trebia (December 218 BCE)
Romans fall back from the Ticinus to Placentia (218 BCE)
chapters.text: Rome expected to fight in Spain and Africa, but in 218 BCE Hannibal marched from New Carthage, past Saguntum, which he had taken the year before, across the Pyrenees, the Rhône and, by late autumn, the Alps. In the Po valley the Gauls rose against Rome; Hannibal took the chief town of the Taurini, beat the Roman cavalry at the Ticinus and destroyed a Roman army at the Trebia in December, although the new Roman colony of Placentia held out. Meanwhile a Roman army landed at Emporion and won a foothold around Tarraco.

chapters.title: Trasimene and Cannae
arrows: Hannibal crosses the Apennines and the Arno marshes to Trasimene (217 BCE)
Hannibal marches through Picenum to Apulia and raids Campania (217 BCE)
Hannibal seizes the Roman depot at Cannae (216 BCE)
Roman consuls march to Canusium and Cannae (216 BCE)
chapters.text: In spring 217 BCE Hannibal crossed the Apennines and ambushed a Roman army beside Lake Trasimene on 21 June. The dictator Fabius then shadowed him without giving battle while Hannibal raided Apulia and Campania. In 216 BCE Rome sent its largest army yet, and on 2 August at Cannae Hannibal surrounded and destroyed it; the survivors gathered at Canusium. The colored circle shows the ground held by Hannibal's army as it moved, not a conquered province.

chapters.title: Italy divided
arrows: Hannibal seizes Tarentum (212 BCE)
Roman armies close in on Capua (212 BCE)
Hannibal's march on Rome (211 BCE)
chapters.text: After Cannae much of southern Italy went over to Hannibal: Capua, the second city of Italy, many Samnites and Lucanians, the Bruttians, and in summer 215 BCE the port of Locri. Rome refused to make peace, held Nola and other strongholds, and kept armies in the field. Hannibal seized the city of Tarentum in 212 BCE, but Roman armies besieged Capua; in 211 BCE he marched to the walls of Rome to draw them away, failed, and Capua surrendered.

chapters.title: Syracuse and Sicily
arrows: Marcellus lays siege to Syracuse (213 BCE)
Himilco lands and takes Agrigentum (213 BCE)
chapters.text: When Syracuse broke its alliance with Rome and sided with Carthage in 214 BCE, Marcellus besieged it by land and sea, held off for months by the war machines of Archimedes. A Carthaginian army under Himilco landed in 213 BCE and took Agrigentum. The Romans stormed Syracuse in 212 BCE and sacked it, killing Archimedes, and in 210 BCE Agrigentum was betrayed to them, ending Carthage's hopes in Sicily.

chapters.title: Scipio wins Spain
arrows: Scipio's march on New Carthage (209 BCE)
Scipio marches to Ilipa (206 BCE)
chapters.text: In 211 BCE both Scipio brothers were killed on the upper Baetis and Rome clung to the coast around Tarraco. Their son and nephew, the young Publius Cornelius Scipio, marched south and stormed New Carthage, the Carthaginian capital in Spain, early in 209 BCE. He beat Hasdrubal Barca at Baecula in 208 BCE and the last Carthaginian armies at Ilipa in 206 BCE, after which Castulo and the rest of Carthaginian Spain fell to Rome.

chapters.title: Hasdrubal and the Metaurus
arrows: Hasdrubal Barca crosses Gaul and the Alps to the Po (208–207 BCE)
Hasdrubal marches south along the Adriatic (207 BCE)
Nero's forced march from Apulia to the Metaurus (207 BCE)
chapters.text: Hasdrubal Barca slipped out of Spain, wintered in Gaul and crossed the Alps in spring 207 BCE to join his brother, gathering Gallic recruits; the colony of Placentia again held out. He marched down the Adriatic coast towards Umbria, but the consul Claudius Nero secretly brought troops north from Apulia. At the Metaurus river, in June 207 BCE, the two Roman armies destroyed Hasdrubal's army and he was killed.

chapters.title: Scipio in Africa and Zama
arrows: Scipio sails from Lilybaeum to Africa (204 BCE)
Hannibal sails from Croton to Africa (203 BCE)
Hannibal marches inland to Zama (202 BCE)
Scipio marches up the Bagradas valley (202 BCE)
chapters.text: In 204 BCE Scipio landed in Africa and fortified a camp, Castra Cornelia, near Utica, which held out against him. In 203 BCE he burned the Carthaginian and Numidian camps and won at the Great Plains, so Carthage recalled Hannibal, who landed with his veterans and gathered his army at Hadrumetum. At Zama in 202 BCE Scipio, with Masinissa's Numidian cavalry, defeated Hannibal, and in spring 201 BCE Carthage accepted Rome's terms.

battles.name: Battle of Cissa
battles.casualties: c. 8,000 Carthaginians killed or captured; Roman losses unknown

battles.name: Battle of the Trebia
battles.casualties: c. 20,000 Romans killed and many captured; several thousand Carthaginian infantry lost

battles.name: Battle of Lake Trasimene
battles.casualties: 15,000 Romans killed and 6,000–10,000 captured; 1,500–2,500 Carthaginians killed

battles.name: Battle of Cannae
battles.casualties: 67,500–80,000 Romans killed or captured; 5,700–8,000 Carthaginians killed

battles.name: Siege of Syracuse
battles.casualties: Over 5,000 Syracusan soldiers and many civilians killed; Roman losses heavy

battles.name: Battle of the Upper Baetis
battles.casualties: 21,000–22,000 Romans and allies killed or captured, including both Scipio brothers

battles.name: Storming of New Carthage
battles.casualties: The garrison of about 1,000 soldiers and 2,000 armed townsmen killed or captured

battles.name: Battle of Ilipa
battles.casualties: c. 7,000 Romans killed; Carthaginian losses far heavier (ancient figures over 48,000 killed or captured)

battles.name: Battle of the Metaurus
battles.casualties: c. 10,000 Carthaginians killed and 5,400 captured, with Hasdrubal; 2,000–8,000 Romans killed

battles.name: Battle of Zama
battles.casualties: c. 20,000 Carthaginians killed and 20,000 captured; at least 1,500 Romans killed
